design_detail: Clinical case series from a dysmorphology unit (Department of Pediatrics, University of Washington, Seattle): eight unrelated children (five girls, three boys; three Native American, three Black, two White) born to mothers with chronic alcoholism who drank heavily throughout pregnancy, examined by two dysmorphologists (K. J., D. W. S.) and, for development, by a psychologist (A. P. S.) with standard infant and child scales. Four children were first recognised as sharing a pattern; two more were found because they had its features, and two because their mothers had chronic alcoholism. Growth, head size and palpebral fissure length are compared with published norms; there is no comparison group and no count of children examined who did not have the pattern. The paper does not use the name fetal alcohol syndrome; it speaks of "this syndrome" (p. 1270).
can_establish: That eight children born to mothers with chronic alcoholism who drank heavily throughout pregnancy shared a recognisable pattern: growth deficiency from before birth without later catch-up, small heads, short palpebral fissures, and mid-face, joint, palmar-crease and heart anomalies in varying combinations, with developmental delay. As a description it defines the pattern and raises the hypothesis that heavy drinking in pregnancy causes it.
cannot_establish: That alcohol caused the pattern (there is no comparison group, and undernutrition, smoking, other drugs, poverty, genetic causes and the postnatal home were not measured or controlled); how often children of mothers who drink heavily are affected (no denominator: possible mildly affected children were deliberately left out and two children were selected because they had the features); whether any lower amount of drinking carries a risk (amounts and timing were not recorded); or outcomes beyond early childhood (the oldest child was tested at 57 months).

sample.recruitment: Clinic and referral: children evaluated at the Dysmorphology Unit, Department of Pediatrics, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle. How the first four came to attention is not stated beyond their being children of mothers with alcoholism brought together for evaluation (Clinical Findings › Methods of Patient Ascertainment, 1st paragraph, p. 1267). The acknowledgements credit a nurse working with mothers with chronic alcoholism for much of the data, another physician for arranging the evaluation of some of the children, and Akron Children's Hospital for information on patient 5, whom D. W. S. evaluated personally (p. 1271).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: The mother met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism and drank excessively throughout the pregnancy (p. 1267). The authors state that they set out the pattern in the more severely affected children and purposely did not include possible mildly affected cases (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 1271). No other criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: Five girls and three boys (case reports, pp. 1267–1268); three Native American (American Indian), three Black and two White (Table II, p. 1268); age at developmental testing 3 to 57 months (Table III, p. 1270). From Table I (p. 1267): mothers aged 22 to 40 at the birth (mean 31.7); each child was the 3rd to 7th born in the family; gestational age 34 to 44 weeks (mean 38); birth weight 1550 to 2500 g (mean 2034); birth length 38 to 47 cm (mean 43.6); breech presentation 3 of 8. All the families were on welfare, with parents' education from 8th grade to college and occupations from unskilled to professional (p. 1271). Six children had been admitted to hospital for failure to thrive, and three had been placed in foster care (p. 1269).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (a single evaluation with growth records). Data are incomplete for some children: several maternal history items unknown for patients 2 and 5, weight change in pregnancy unknown for patients 2 and 3 (Table I); motor age not estimated for patients 1 and 5, an IQ or developmental index missing for patient 5, and social maturity recorded for four children only (Table III); Figure 4 shows growth for patients 2 to 8 only; head circumference at 1 year was available for six (p. 1269).
sample.selection_effects: Ascertainment partly on the outcome: after four children were recognised as alike, two more were found because they had the same features, and possible mildly affected children were deliberately excluded, so the uniformity of the pattern is partly built in by the selection. Only two children were ascertained through maternal alcoholism alone, and the number of children of mothers with alcoholism who were examined and found unaffected is not reported. Some siblings are described only as alleged to be normal (p. 1271). All the children came from families on welfare, and six had been admitted for failure to thrive.

exposure.measurement: Maternal alcoholism by the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria; how the criteria were applied, and from what sources the histories came, is not stated. Drinking during pregnancy is described only as excessive throughout. History of delirium tremens in 5 of 6 mothers with data (the mothers of patients 1 and 7 were in hospital with delirium tremens during the pregnancy, and patient 3 was born while her mother was in an alcoholic stupor), cirrhosis in 2 of 6 and nutritional anaemia in 2 of 6 (p. 1267; Table I).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No amounts, beverages, frequency or timing of drinking in pregnancy are reported, and no standard drink or grams are used. Duration of maternal alcoholism 2+ to 23 years (mean 9.4) (Table I, p. 1267).
exposure.polysubstance: None of the mothers was known to be addicted to any other drug (p. 1267); smoking, and use of other drugs short of addiction, are not reported. Maternal nutrition is documented only as nutritional anaemia (2 of 6 with data) and weight change during pregnancy (a loss of 1 to 15 lb in four mothers, a gain of 19 and 30 lb in two, unknown in two) (Table I).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Postnatal environment: patient 1 had been in foster care from birth and patient 3 from 2 to 4 years of age; three children in all had been in foster care (pp. 1269, 1271); the others presumably remained with their families, which the paper does not state.

comparison.controls: None. Measurements are compared with published norms: palpebral fissure length with a mean curve for White children from Chouke (1929) (Figure 3); length and weight with the 50th percentile of the Stuart growth charts (Figure 4); head circumference with 2 SD below the mean for normal males from Nellhaus (1968) (Figure 5); daily weight gain with two Seattle reference groups by personal communication (p. 1269); development with the norms of each test (Table III).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Maternal nutrition (only partly recorded), smoking, other drug use, prenatal care, infections, prematurity (gestational age 34 to 44 weeks), genetic causes (chromosomes were studied only in patients 1 and 7, both normal) and socioeconomic deprivation (all the families on welfare) were not measured systematically. The authors argue against undernutrition (length more affected than weight; the pattern not previously recognised in children of undernourished women without alcoholism; no catch-up despite adequate calories) and against the home environment (two children in foster care did no better), but these are arguments, not comparisons (pp. 1270–1271).

outcomes.instruments: Clinical dysmorphology examination; palpebral fissure length measured from the medial to the lateral canthus (p. 1267; Figure 3); length, weight and head circumference plotted against published norms (Figures 4 and 5); cardiac findings from murmurs, one cardiac catheterisation (patient 2) and clinical evaluation (patient 4); chromosome studies in patients 1 and 7; development by the Bayley infant scales (motor and mental), the Stanford-Binet scale form L-M, the Denver developmental scale (patient 5) and the Vineland social maturity scale completed with one or both parents (Table III, p. 1270).
outcomes.validity_norms: The norms are not matched to the children: palpebral fissure length against a mean curve without a range for White children, although six of the eight were Native American or Black; head circumference against norms for boys for all eight, although five were girls. Motor age is called an estimate only because of the test's low ceiling, and the normal range for development is not defined (p. 1270).
outcomes.operationalization: Each feature recorded as present or absent by the examiners (Table II); microcephaly as head circumference below the 3rd percentile for gestational age at birth; growth deficiency as length and weight below norms without catch-up; developmental delay as test performance outside a normal range that is not defined (pp. 1268–1270).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests. Table II records 10 features and Table III five developmental measures.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. The examiners knew of the mothers' alcoholism (the basis of ascertainment for two children) and had recognised the pattern before ascertaining two further children by it; one psychologist tested seven of the eight children (p. 1269).

analysis.effect_sizes: None (descriptive counts). Table II (p. 1268): developmental delay 8/8, microcephaly 7/8, prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency 8/8 each, short palpebral fissures 8/8, maxillary hypoplasia with relative prognathism 7/8, epicanthal folds 4/8, joint anomalies 5/8, altered palmar crease pattern 6/8, cardiac anomaly 5/8. Growth (p. 1269): mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks' gestation against a mean gestational age of 38 weeks; after 1 year of age, average linear growth 65% and weight gain 38% of normal; mean daily weight gain 9 g against 26.6 g and 24.4 g in two Seattle reference groups. Head circumference below the 3rd percentile for gestational age at birth in 7 of 8, and at 1 year below it for both height age and chronological age in 5 of 6 with data (p. 1269). Development (Table III, p. 1270): IQ or mental development index 83, 79, 75, 70, 59 and 57, and below 50, in seven children; mental age 2+ to 44 months at ages 3 to 57 months; fine motor dysfunction in 5 of 6 tested; repetitive self-stimulating behaviour in 5 (p. 1270).
analysis.selective_reporting: The authors deliberately describe the more severely affected children and leave out possible mildly affected cases (p. 1271); siblings are described only in general terms; the paper does not say how many children of mothers with alcoholism were seen in all.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Eight children of mothers with chronic alcoholism, examined by dysmorphologists who knew the mothers' history and selected partly for their features, shared growth deficiency from before birth, small heads, short palpebral fissures and developmental delay, with mid-face, joint, palmar-crease and heart anomalies in some. There was no comparison group, no count of unaffected children and no record of how much the mothers drank.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary calls the report "the first reported association between maternal alcoholism and aberrant morphogenesis" (p. 1267); the Discussion says it points strongly to such an association and ends that "the data are sufficient to establish that maternal alcoholism can cause serious aberrant fetal development" (p. 1271). Gaps: (1) a case series without a comparison group or a denominator shows that the features occurred together in these children, not an association in the epidemiological sense and not causation; (2) the similarity of the pattern, which the authors take to suggest a single cause (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 1270), is partly produced by the selection (two children ascertained by the features, milder cases excluded); (3) the alternative explanations (undernutrition, smoking, other drugs, poverty, genetic causes, the postnatal home) are argued against with reasoning and with two children in foster care, not measured, and the authors themselves say the effects of the socioeconomic situation and of continuing maternal alcoholism on development are hard to separate (p. 1271); (4) no amount or timing of drinking was recorded, so nothing in the paper bears on lower amounts; (5) the claim to be first is the authors' own and was not checked for this card. Against this, the Discussion names the alternative causes openly and calls the attribution of the developmental findings to early brain morphogenesis tempting rather than shown (p. 1271).

timeline.event: Ulleland (a co-author) called attention to growth deficiency and developmental delay in children of mothers with alcoholism (cited as ref. 1, p. 1267; not read); whether any of the eight children were in that report is not stated.
This report: the pattern of malformation in eight children; the round's list calls it the first description of fetal alcohol syndrome, a name the paper itself does not use.
Henderson, Gray & Brocklehurst, systematic review of low-to-moderate prenatal alcohol exposure and pregnancy outcome (with an erratum), on the round's list (Tier C; not read).

Flak et al. (2014), meta-analysis of mild, moderate and binge prenatal exposure and child neuropsychological outcomes, and Mamluk et al. (2017), systematic review and meta-analysis of low consumption in pregnancy, both on the round's list (Tier C; not read).
Hoyme et al., updated clinical guidelines for diagnosing fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, on the round's list (Tier C; not read).

Popova et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of drinking in pregnancy and of fetal alcohol syndrome, and Lange et al., meta-analysis of the prevalence of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: both in this round (Tier A), read by another reader.
May et al., prevalence of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders in four US communities, on the round's list (Tier C; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The round's list describes this paper as the first description of fetal alcohol syndrome. Later work on the list (diagnostic guidelines, prevalence studies and meta-analyses, none read for this card) treats the syndrome as a diagnosable condition, so the description was taken up; hence the status partially replicated. Whether heavy prenatal alcohol exposure causes the pattern, how often it follows such exposure, and what happens at lower amounts are questions for those later studies' cards, not for this one. Claims may cite this paper for the original description and for the frequency of each feature in these eight children only.

funding.funder: Maternal and Child Health Services, Health Services and Mental Administration (as printed), Department of Health, Education and Welfare project 913; National Institutes of Health grant HD 05961; National Foundation-March of Dimes (acknowledgements, p. 1271).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement).
funding.affiliations_note: Dysmorphology Unit, Department of Pediatrics, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle. The prior observation the paper builds on is its co-author's (Ulleland, 1972, ref. 1). Information on patient 5 came from Akron Children's Hospital (p. 1271).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of pregnancies with drinking recorded by amount and timing, from none to heavy, and with smoking, other drugs, nutrition and socioeconomic position measured, whose children are examined at birth and through childhood by examiners who do not know the exposure, using measurements against sex- and population-specific norms: it would show how often the pattern occurs at each level of drinking and whether it is specific to alcohol.

domains.note: Four children recognised first, two more ascertained because they had the features, two because the mother had chronic alcoholism; possible mildly affected children deliberately excluded; no count of children examined (pp. 1267, 1271).
Maternal alcoholism by the 1972 criteria, but no amount, beverage or timing of drinking in pregnancy; several history items unknown for two mothers; the sources of the histories are not stated.

Present-or-absent clinical judgments; palpebral fissures measured and standard developmental tests used, but norms not matched to sex or population (norms for boys for five girls; a mean for White children for six Native American or Black children), three of five cardiac anomalies presumed from murmurs that disappeared, and the normal range of development undefined.
The same two dysmorphologists, who knew the mothers' alcoholism and had already recognised the pattern, examined the children; no independent or blinded rating.
No comparison group of children of mothers without alcoholism from similar circumstances (all the families were on welfare); siblings described only in general terms.

Undernutrition, smoking, other drugs, prematurity, genetic causes and the postnatal home were not measured or controlled; the authors argue against some of them without comparison data (pp. 1270–1271).

The closing sentence says the data establish that maternal alcoholism can cause the disorder, beyond what eight selected cases can show, although the Discussion elsewhere presents the causes as possibilities (pp. 1270–1271).

Patient 5 was evaluated differently from the stated method, patient 4 is listed under two developmental tests, a row labelled social quotient is given in months, and the norms used for the head-circumference statements are not named (reporting issues 1 to 3 and 6).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a case series (METHODS §5.3); the editors' domains above describe its limits, and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The paper is the original clinical description of a pattern in eight children and is cited for that: the features, their frequency in these eight, and the authors' hypotheses. It is never cited for how often heavy drinking in pregnancy leads to the pattern, for any amount of drinking, or, on its own, for causation.

S.): four were first recognised as sharing a pattern of altered growth and morphogenesis, two more were ascertained because they had the features found in the first four, and two because their mothers had chronic alcoholism.

key_findings.finding: All eight had prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency: with a mean gestational age of 38 weeks, mean birth length and weight were at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks, so length was more affected than weight. None showed catch-up growth, either during hospital admissions for failure to thrive (six children), with adequate calorie intake recorded, or in foster care (three children). After 1 year of age, average linear growth was 65% of normal and weight gain 38%; mean daily weight gain was 9 g against 26.6 g in upper-middle-class Seattle children and 24.4 g in high-risk children in a local maternal and infant care programme.
key_findings.note: The text layer renders 26.6 and 24.4 with wrong characters; both read on the rendered page. The reference values come from a personal communication (ref. 3), and the period over which the rates were computed is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Head circumference was below the 3rd percentile for gestational age at birth in seven of the eight children, and by 1 year below the 3rd percentile for height age as well as chronological age in five of the six with data.
key_findings.note: Figure 5 plots head circumference against a band 2 SD below the mean for normal males (Nellhaus) for all eight children, five of them girls; the shaded band is not visible in this scanned copy, and values were not extracted from the figure.

key_findings.finding: Table III, by patient (age at testing; mental age; IQ or mental development index, in months where applicable): 1, 14, 10, 59; 2, 3, 2+, 83; 3, 57, 44, 75; 4, 46, 26, 57; 5, 18, 11, not given; 6, 40, 32, 79; 7, 48, 34, 70; 8, 34, 19, below 50. Motor age 2 to 31 months in six children; social maturity (Vineland, from parents) 23 to 36 months in four. The authors report that none of the children performed within the normal range, that social and motor performance matched mental age more than chronological age, fine motor dysfunction in five of the six tested, and repetitive self-stimulating behaviour such as head rolling, head banging or rocking in five.

Chromosome studies, done in patients 1 and 7, were normal.

key_findings.finding: The authors take the similarity of the pattern to suggest a single cause, most likely an effect of maternal alcoholism; they name direct ethanol toxicity as the most obvious possibility, with acetaldehyde or an unknown agent in the beverages, and maternal undernutrition or a specific nutrient deficiency as alternatives. They argue against undernutrition because this degree of prenatal growth deficiency and this pattern had not been recognised in children of undernourished women without alcoholism, and because length was more affected than weight, the reverse of generalised maternal undernutrition.

key_findings.finding: All the families were on welfare, with parents' education ranging from 8th grade to college; patient 1 (in foster care from birth) and patient 3 (in foster care from 2 to 4 years) did not perform better. The authors state that it is difficult to determine how far the socioeconomic situation or continuing maternal alcoholism affected development, and that the postnatal growth deficiency persisted despite adequate intake in hospital or foster care.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say all eight children were evaluated at the same time by the same two observers (p. 1267), but the acknowledgements say that information on patient 5 was supplied by Akron Children's Hospital and that D. W. S. evaluated this child personally (p. 1271); patient 5 is also the one child whose development was not tested by A. P. S. and was assessed with the Denver scale (pp. 1269–1270).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the eight children was ascertained and assessed differently from the others, which the Methods do not say.
